$meta.name: doinstruct Ask design tokens
$meta.description: The INTENT layer. tokens.css holds the same values as Tailwind v4 `@theme` declarations and is what generates the utility classes. Agents: read this file to learn why a value is what it is, read tokens.css to learn what to type.
$meta.relationship: Neither file generates the other. They are two views of one system and they drifted apart badly once already: at v0.1.0 eleven of the eighteen hexes here were stale, still carrying a first-draft palette that had since been corrected for brand accuracy and for the 7:1 floor. Nothing caught it, because 'source of truth' was a claim in prose. scripts/check-tokens.mjs now fails the build if a colour appears in one file and not the other.
$meta.derivedFrom: doinstruct's own Webflow swatch system, read from their production stylesheet. Exact values, not eyeballed. Divergences are marked with `divergence` and a reason. Do not 'correct' them back to brand values.
$meta.contrastPolicy: Every text pair clears 7:1, every border and chart mark clears 3:1, and the sequential scale is checked for ordered steps rather than a flat floor. Enforced by scripts/check-contrast.mjs on every `npm run check`. Two brand swatches did not meet the text floor and were darkened; both are recorded below.
$meta.registers: Two. The floor is a worker's own phone or a shared terminal in a hygiene zone: gloves, 85-95 dB, washdown glare to dim cold store, no login. The office is a shift lead or QHSE manager at a desk: mouse, monitor, normal light. Tokens marked `register: office` are forbidden on the floor, enforced by scripts/check-register.mjs.

ink.usage: Text on light surfaces; fill for the primary action's label; the inverse surface.

yellow.note: Their system calls this yellow, not lime. Using their vocabulary.
yellow.usage: RESERVED. Exactly one element per screen may be yellow: the primary voice action. brand.ink on brand.yellow measures 15.64:1.
yellow.rule: Yellow never carries text meaning, never carries status, and never appears in a chart. It is 1.1:1 against cream, so it cannot be a mark. If yellow appears twice on a screen, the screen is wrong.

unusedSwatches.note: Present in their brand, deliberately not used here. Exempt from scripts/check-tokens.mjs by name.
unusedSwatches.reason: The third near-black green. Two inverse surfaces is enough to build a hierarchy on the dark ground; a third would only dilute it.
unusedSwatches.$formerly: --swatch--green (#153327) was listed here too, on the reasoning that one inverse surface was enough. That held while the dark ground was reserved for the listening state. Once it became a real surface across both registers it needed a raised step, and their own swatch was already the right colour.

sunken.note: Derived. They have no equivalent swatch.

inverse.usage: The brand ground. Floor chrome and entry screens, the office rail, and full-bleed states such as listening.
inverse.$change: This used to be reserved for full-bleed states. Reserving it meant the product used doinstruct's colours as ink and never as ground, so it could not look like their product: a cream document with black type and one yellow button. Dark green is now a surface people spend time on, and cream is where they read.

inverseRaised.usage: Cards and rows sitting on the dark ground.

surface.$rule: Fill surfaces, do not outline them. Outlined boxes on a flat ground read as a wireframe no matter how correct the spacing is. This was the single biggest visual failure of the first version.

secondary.reason: Theirs measures 4.6:1 on off-white. Fine for marketing, below the floor for a plant floor. Darkened, hue preserved.

onInverseMuted.reason: 9.6:1 on the dark ground and 7.3:1 on the raised one. The same job as text.secondary, held to the same floor, on the other side of the system.

text.$rule: No text token below 7:1 exists. AA (4.5:1) is insufficient under washdown glare and in dim cold-store lighting. Measured ratios live in the output of scripts/check-contrast.mjs rather than here, because a number written into a document is a number that goes stale.

status.$note: Each status ships with its own tinted surface so the pair clears 7:1 together. All four were darkened from a first pass that failed at 5.4 to 6.1:1.

stop.rule: Only for hazard, lockout/tagout, and refusal-to-answer states. Never for validation errors, never for 'delete', never decorative. A worker must be able to trust that red means stop working.

caution.usage: Requires a qualified person, PPE required, verify before acting.

pending.usage: Escalated and waiting on a human.

status.$rule: Status is never a chart series and a chart series is never status. Every status ships with an icon and a label, so colour is never the only carrier. That pairing is also the mitigation for the one measured collision in this system: chart series 3 (violet) sits 15.2 from status pending in OKLab, just over the floor, and they are both blue-violet.

border.$note: Three jobs, three tokens. Every border in this system is 2px; the tokens carry colour, not width.

hairline.usage: Decorative edge on a filled surface.
hairline.reason: Never the sole carrier of a boundary. In normal light the fill does that job; in high contrast this token flips to pure black and takes over. The exemption is a statement about what it is for, not a threshold quietly lowered.

hairlineInverse.usage: Decorative edge on the dark ground.
hairlineInverse.reason: Same argument as its light twin: fill carries the boundary, and at high contrast it flips to pure white and takes over.

strong.note: Unchanged from brand. It is non-text UI, so 3:1 is the correct floor and it clears it.

focus.reason: Thick because the device may be operated with a stylus or a knuckle, and because focus is the only affordance available to a screen-reader user in a noisy environment.
focus.$rule: Focus does NOT change between registers. Density is an environment decision; focus is an accessibility one, and the office does not get a thinner ring for looking tidier.

highContrast.description: Not a preference, but a lighting condition. Toggled by the user, persists per device.
highContrast.$rule: High contrast works through token overrides alone. NEVER add a blanket rule such as `[data-contrast='high'] * { border-width: 2px }`: Tailwind's preflight sets `border: 0 solid` on every element, so a blanket width hands a visible border to every div and paragraph on the page. This happened here.
highContrast.$chartRule: The series and scale colours are not overridden, because both sets were validated against #FFFFFF as well as #FCFBF8. What changes is the chart, not the palette: every mark prints its value as text, so colour drops to decoration and the number carries the meaning.

dataviz.$origin: These are not brand colours and could not be. doinstruct's yellow is 1.1:1 on cream and their greens are near-black, so neither sits in the OKLCH lightness band a chart fill needs. The palette is built beside the brand, sharing its temperature, rather than extracted from it.
dataviz.$validation: Checked with the dataviz method's validator against both surfaces (#FCFBF8 and the high-contrast #FFFFFF): OKLCH lightness band, chroma floor, protanopia and deuteranopia separation, normal-vision floor, and 3:1 contrast. Worst adjacent pair is series 4 against series 5 at ΔE 12.5 simulated and 23.1 unsimulated, against targets of 8 and 15.

series.$rule: Fixed order, assigned in sequence, never cycled. A sixth series folds into 'Other' or the chart becomes small multiples. Colour follows the entity, never its rank, so a filter that removes a series must not repaint the survivors.
series.$allPairsCap: Three. Scatter, bubble and small-multiple forms, where any two marks can end up side by side, may use series 1 to 3 only. Series 4 and series 2 collapse to ΔE 1.0 under deuteranopia when they are not adjacent in a stack, which the adjacent-pair test cannot see.

scale.$usage: Magnitude. One hue, light to dark, taking series 1's hue per the convention that the sequential ramp uses the first categorical slot.
scale.$note: Step 3 is a near-neighbour of series 1 without being identical, and that is not sloppiness. Unifying them fails the categorical chroma floor at 0.098 against 0.10. The spacing a readable ramp needs and the saturation a series identity needs do not land on the same value.
scale.$check: Monotone lightness with adjacent ΔL at least 0.06, light end visible at 2:1, dark end clearing the 3:1 mark floor. Holding every step to 3:1 would be the wrong test and would produce a ramp with no light end.

diverging.$absent: Nothing in this product encodes polarity; the office screens count things and rank things. When one arrives it is series 1 against series 2, teal to rust, with a neutral grey midpoint, because those are the only two poles here that read as opposite. Adding it now would be a token nobody uses.

chrome.$note: No new tokens. A gridline is a hairline and a baseline is a border; inventing chart-specific greys would be two more values to keep in sync for no gain.

v2.$status: PROPOSAL. A rebrand concept, shipped as a working theme rather than a mood board: `[data-theme='v2']` in tokens.css, every value validated by scripts/check-contrast.mjs against the same pairs and the same thresholds as the shipped palette.
v2.$thesis: A brand for people who cannot rely on language should be built the way industrial safety signage is: engineered to be understood at a glance, by anyone, in any condition. So every value here was SOLVED to a contrast floor along an OKLCH hue rather than picked and then checked.

$whatChanges.accentCanWork: doinstruct's yellow is 1.1:1 on their off-white, so it can never be text, a border, a chart mark or a status. Their most recognisable asset is confined to one button per screen. The v2 accent is a solved teal clearing 7:1 as text on paper, so one colour carries the primary action, links, focus and a chart series.
$whatChanges.yellowIsNotDeleted: It moves to brand expression: large fields, print, the wordmark, marketing. 1.1:1 is nobody's problem on a billboard. What it stops doing is product work it was never able to do.
$whatChanges.paletteHasAMiddle: The shipped system is near-black greens, an acid accent and off-whites with nothing usable between. --swatch--mid-green measures 4.6:1 and --swatch--light-green 1.65:1; both had to be darkened to build anything. The v2 ramps are perceptually even, so a mid-tone is available and predictable.
$whatChanges.greenBecomesMeaning: The ground is warm ink rather than near-black green. Green is promoted from decoration to meaning: verified, current, safe. Which is what green already means to someone standing on a plant floor.
$whatChanges.tokensNamedByRole: `--color-yellow` is named after appearance, which is fine until a theme changes the appearance. v2 introduced `--color-accent` and `--color-accent-fg`, and migrating the components to them was the single clearest evidence that the shipped tokens were named for how they look rather than what they do.

$openQuestions: Retiring the acid yellow from product surfaces is the biggest risk in this proposal. It is the most recognisable thing doinstruct owns and this trades recognition for capability. Worth testing with their customers rather than asserting.

The safety palette collides with any brand that uses signal colours. This is why the accent is teal: red, amber and green are spoken for, and a brand accent that looks like a warning is a brand accent that will eventually be mistaken for one.
v2.$whatBuildingItTaught: The first accent was solved to 7:1 as text on paper, which made it a deep teal: correct by every number and wrong on the screen, because the primary voice action has to be unmissable across a room and a dark fill is the one thing it must never be. The yellow it replaces was salient before it was legible. An accent needs two steps, a bright one for fills and a dark one for text, which is what a ramp is for. This is the argument for building a rebrand as a theme before writing it up.

min.reason: 44px assumes a bare fingertip. A cut-resistant glove has a contact patch of roughly 14-16mm and no proprioceptive feedback. 64px is the floor here, and nothing interactive on the device may be smaller.

primary.reason: The push-to-talk target must be hittable without looking, by someone holding a part in their other hand.

spacing.reason: Minimum gap between adjacent targets. Gloved mis-taps are the dominant input error, and an accidental tap on a safety-critical control is not recoverable by undo.

workMaxWidth.usage: Screens holding sentences in two columns: the queue and the composer.
workMaxWidth.reason: Past roughly 1400px a question becomes a line of text with a hundred characters of whitespace after it, and the eye has to travel the width of a monitor to get from the machine name to the wait.

readMaxWidth.usage: A single column of prose. The knowledge record.
readMaxWidth.reason: One measure, one column. Wider is not more readable, it is just further to travel back to the start of the next line.

desk.$fluid: The shell has no cap and Coverage has none either. Coverage is charts, and a chart uses width without its labels getting any longer. Caps are applied left-aligned rather than centred, so content stays flush with the header band above and the rail beside it.

control.reason: A mouse cursor is one pixel and a trackpad gives proprioceptive feedback, so the glove reasoning does not apply. 36px sits comfortably above WCAG 2.2 AA's 24px minimum.

row.reason: Taller than a control because a row holds two lines and is itself the click target.

spacing.reason: Minimum gap between adjacent targets at a desk. A mis-click is recoverable and a supervisor scanning forty rows needs the density.

breakpointXs.reason: Tailwind's smallest is 40rem, wider than every phone. The office rail needs one decision below it: under 26rem, three labelled destinations plus a count stop fitting a row, and the icons come off rather than the words.

width.reason: Wide enough for the asset ID at a size someone can read out over 90 dB of line noise when the camera will not focus.

qr.reason: The smallest QR a mid-range phone reads reliably at arm's length in a badly lit plant. Below roughly 25mm you are relying on the worker getting close to the machine, which is the thing the label exists to avoid.

label.$note: Millimetres because this one is not a screen. It gets printed, laminated and stuck to something that is hosed down every shift.

floor.reason: Read at arm's length, often through safety glasses, frequently by workers over 50. On the device, `meta` at 14px exists only for timestamps and audit references, never for instructions.

office.reason: Seated, roughly 60cm from a monitor. `meta` at 14px is legitimate body text here, for table cells and axis labels.
office.$rule: One scale, two floors. The register changes which end of the type scale you may use, not the values in it. No office-only type tokens exist, and adding some would be how a design system quietly becomes two design systems.

family.sans: system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif
family.$note: System stack only. Zero webfont bytes, and identical behaviour on a throttled 3G connection and a five-year-old Android. doinstruct's own site uses Manrope; matching it would cost a network round trip on the exact device this product has to work on, so the divergence is deliberate.
family.$registers: Both. The office does not get a webfont for looking smarter, because a two-register system with two typefaces is two systems.

meta.usage: Floor: timestamps and audit IDs only. Office: table cells, axis labels, legends.

scale.$note: Negative tracking appears only above 28px. Below that it costs legibility for readers who are decoding rather than reading, which is most of the people this product is for.

typography.figures: Proportional by default. `tabular-nums` is reserved for columns that must align vertically: table rows, axis ticks, and any number a supervisor scans down rather than reads.
typography.$rule: Maximum 65 characters per line. Multilingual: German compounds and Romanian diacritics both overflow. Every text container must wrap, never truncate. Truncation of a safety instruction is a defect.

xs.usage: The data end of a chart bar, and nothing else. Square against the baseline, because a bar rounded at both ends lies about where it starts.

radius.$rule: Always name the step. Bare `rounded`, `rounded-t` and `rounded-b` resolve to Tailwind's own 0.25rem rather than to this system, because the theme defines the steps but no bare `--radius`. A rounded container must also clip its children with `overflow-hidden`, or a child's own background will sit outside the parent's corner. Both have bitten this project, and both compiled clean.

motion.$rule: Nothing animates longer than 200ms and nothing animates position. A worker glancing away for two seconds must find the screen where they left it. All motion respects prefers-reduced-motion.

raised.usage: Chrome that content scrolls under: sticky headers, toolbars.

overlay.usage: Something genuinely detached: popovers, tooltips, dialogs.

elevation.$tint: Brand ink rather than black, so a shadow stays inside the palette instead of greying it.
elevation.$floorRule: No shadows on the floor, and this is not squeamishness about depth. Under direct washdown lighting a soft shadow is invisible, and it vanishes completely when a customer prints a screen to a laminated card for the line, which they do. Hierarchy there comes from surface colour and border.
elevation.$meaningRule: A shadow says 'this floats'. It never says anything else and never carries information, because it is removed entirely at high contrast.
